front_blocks.md: What is **electromagnetic induction**? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: **Electromagnetic induction** is the effect where an **e.m.f. is induced** in a conductor whenever there is **relative movement** between the conductor and a **magnetic field**.

cards.front_md: What is **electromagnetic induction**? **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md: **Electromagnetic induction** is the effect where an **e.m.f. is induced** in a conductor whenever there is **relative movement** between the conductor and a **magnetic field**.

front_blocks.md: How can an e.m.f. be induced in a wire? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: An e.m.f. can be induced in a wire by moving it through a magnetic field, so that the wire **cuts** the magnetic field lines.

cards.front_md: How can an e.m.f. be induced in a wire? **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md: An e.m.f. can be induced in a wire by moving it through a magnetic field, so that the wire **cuts** the magnetic field lines.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
An e.m.f. can only be induced by moving a conductor in a magnetic field. **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: **False.**
An e.m.f. can also be induced by placing a stationary conductor in a **changing** magnetic field.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

An e.m.f. can only be induced by moving a conductor in a magnetic field. **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md:
**False.**

An e.m.f. can also be induced by placing a stationary conductor in a **changing** magnetic field.

front_blocks.md: What **apparatus** can be used to determine if an e.m.f. has been induced in a conductor? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: A **sensitive voltmeter** can be used to measure the size of the induced e.m.f.
If the conductor is part of a **complete circuit**, the induced **current** can be detected by an **ammeter**.

cards.front_md: What **apparatus** can be used to determine if an e.m.f. has been induced in a conductor? **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md:
A **sensitive voltmeter** can be used to measure the size of the induced e.m.f.

If the conductor is part of a **complete circuit**, the induced **current** can be detected by an **ammeter**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
An e.m.f. is induced when a coil and a bar magnet move in the same direction at the same speed. **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: **False.**
For electromagnetic induction to occur, there must be **relative movement** between the conductor and the magnetic field.
Therefore, an e.m.f. is **not** induced when a coil and a bar magnet move in the same direction at the same speed.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

An e.m.f. is induced when a coil and a bar magnet move in the same direction at the same speed. **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md:
**False.**

For electromagnetic induction to occur, there must be **relative movement** between the conductor and the magnetic field.

Therefore, an e.m.f. is **not** induced when a coil and a bar magnet move in the same direction at the same speed.

front_blocks.md: What **four** factors affect the **size** of an induced e.m.f.? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: The four factors that affect the size of an induced e.m.f. are:

- the **speed** at which the wire, coil or magnet is moved
- the **number of turns** on the coils in the wire
- the **size** of the coils
- the **strength** of the magnetic field

- the **strength** of the magnetic field

front_blocks.md: How can the **direction** of an induced e.m.f. be reversed? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: The direction of an induced e.m.f. can be reversed by:

- reversing the **direction** in which the wire, coil or magnet is moved
- switching the **poles** of the magnet

front_blocks.md: Define **a.c. generator**. **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: An **a.c. generator** is a device which converts energy from **motion** into an **electrical** output.

cards.front_md: Define **a.c. generator**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md: An **a.c. generator** is a device which converts energy from **motion** into an **electrical** output.

front_blocks.md: What is the **output** of an a.c. generator? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: An a.c. generator produces an **alternating e.m.f.**, which causes an **alternating current** to flow.

cards.front_md: What is the **output** of an a.c. generator? **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md: An a.c. generator produces an **alternating e.m.f.**, which causes an **alternating current** to flow.

front_blocks.md: What components make up a simple a.c. generator? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: A simple a.c. generator consists of:

- a **rotating coil** of wire between the poles of a **permanent magnet**
- **slip rings** and **brushes** connected to an external circuit

cards.front_md: What components make up a simple a.c. generator? **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md:

- **slip rings** and **brushes** connected to an external circuit

front_blocks.md: What is the purpose of the **slip rings** in an a.c. generator? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: The purpose of the slip rings is to allow the **alternating current** to flow between the **rotating coil** and the **external circuit**.

cards.front_md: What is the purpose of the **slip rings** in an a.c. generator? **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md: The purpose of the slip rings is to allow the **alternating current** to flow between the **rotating coil** and the **external circuit**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A maximum e.m.f. is induced in an a.c. generator when the coil is moving parallel to the magnetic field. **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: **False.**
A maximum e.m.f. is induced when the coil is in a **horizontal** position and its motion is **perpendicular** to the field.
This is because the greatest number of field lines are cut when the coil moves perpendicular to the field.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

A maximum e.m.f. is induced in an a.c. generator when the coil is moving parallel to the magnetic field. **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md:
**False.**

A maximum e.m.f. is induced when the coil is in a **horizontal** position and its motion is **perpendicular** to the field.

This is because the greatest number of field lines are cut when the coil moves perpendicular to the field.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
There is a point in the rotation of an a.c. generator's coil where no e.m.f. is induced. **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: **True.**
No e.m.f. is induced when the coil is in a **vertical** position and its motion is **parallel** to the field.
This is because no field lines are cut when the coil moves parallel to the field.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

There is a point in the rotation of an a.c. generator's coil where no e.m.f. is induced. **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md:
**True.**

No e.m.f. is induced when the coil is in a **vertical** position and its motion is **parallel** to the field.

This is because no field lines are cut when the coil moves parallel to the field.

front_blocks.md: How often does the direction of the induced e.m.f. reverse as the coil of an a.c. generator rotates? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: The direction of the induced e.m.f. (and current) reverses every **half rotation** of the coil.

cards.front_md: How often does the direction of the induced e.m.f. reverse as the coil of an a.c. generator rotates? **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md: The direction of the induced e.m.f. (and current) reverses every **half rotation** of the coil.

front_blocks.md: What is the shape of the graph of e.m.f. against time for an a.c. generator? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: The graph of e.m.f. against time for an a.c. generator is a **sine** or **cosine** curve, depending on the starting position of the coil:

- starting from a **horizontal** position (maximum e.m.f.), the graph is a **cosine** curve
- starting from a **vertical** position (zero e.m.f.), the graph is a **sine** curve

cards.front_md: What is the shape of the graph of e.m.f. against time for an a.c. generator? **(Extended Tier Only)**

front_blocks.md: How can the size of the induced e.m.f. be **increased** in an a.c. generator? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: In an a.c. generator, the size of the induced e.m.f. can be increased by:

- increasing the **frequency** of rotation of the coil
- increasing the number of **turns** on the coil
- increasing the **strength** of the magnet
- inserting a **soft iron core** into the coil

front_blocks.md: What is the pattern of the magnetic field due to the current in a straight wire? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: The magnetic field due to a current in a straight wire forms **concentric circles** centred on the wire, which get **further apart** with increasing distance from the wire.

cards.front_md: What is the pattern of the magnetic field due to the current in a straight wire? **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md: The magnetic field due to a current in a straight wire forms **concentric circles** centred on the wire, which get **further apart** with increasing distance from the wire.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The magnetic field around a current-carrying straight wire has no poles. **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: **True.**
The **circular** field pattern around a current-carrying wire indicates that the field has **no poles**.

cards.front_md:

front_blocks.md: What rule is used to determine the direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: The **right-hand grip rule** is used to determine the direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire.
Point the **right-hand thumb** in the direction of the (conventional) current; the direction of the **curled fingers** represents the direction of the magnetic field lines.

front_blocks.md: What is the pattern of the magnetic field around a current-carrying solenoid? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: The field lines around a solenoid are similar to those of a **bar magnet**:

- one end of the solenoid becomes a **north** pole and the other a **south** pole
- the field lines **emerge** from the north pole and **return** to the south pole

cards.front_md: What is the pattern of the magnetic field around a current-carrying solenoid? **(Extended Tier Only)**

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
When viewed from the end of a solenoid, the pole is a north pole if the current travels clockwise around the coil. **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: **False.**
The **north** pole forms at the end where the current flows **anticlockwise**, and the **south** pole at the end where the current flows **clockwise**.

cards.front_md:

When viewed from the end of a solenoid, the pole is a north pole if the current travels clockwise around the coil. **(Extended Tier Only)**

front_blocks.md: How can the **strength** of the magnetic field around a straight wire be increased? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: The strength of the magnetic field around a straight wire can be increased by increasing the amount of **current** flowing through the wire.
The field is **strongest near the wire** and becomes weaker further away, shown by the field lines becoming **further apart**.

cards.front_md: How can the **strength** of the magnetic field around a straight wire be increased? **(Extended Tier Only)**

front_blocks.md: What effect does reversing the current have on the magnetic field around a wire or solenoid? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: Reversing the direction of the **current** reverses the **direction** of the magnetic field produced.

cards.front_md: What effect does reversing the current have on the magnetic field around a wire or solenoid? **(Extended Tier Only)**

front_blocks.md: Why does inserting a **soft iron core** into a solenoid produce a stronger magnet? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: The iron core becomes an **induced magnet** when a current flows through the coils.
The magnetic field produced by the solenoid and the iron core together creates a much **stronger** magnet overall — this is how an **electromagnet** works.

cards.front_md: Why does inserting a **soft iron core** into a solenoid produce a stronger magnet? **(Extended Tier Only)**

front_blocks.md: Why does a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experience a force? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: A current-carrying conductor produces its **own magnetic field**.
When this interacts with an **external magnetic field**, the conductor experiences a **force**, which makes it move.

cards.front_md: Why does a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experience a force? **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md:
A current-carrying conductor produces its **own magnetic field**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A current-carrying conductor will only experience a force if the current is parallel to the magnetic field lines. **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: **False.**
A current-carrying conductor will only experience a force if the current through it is **perpendicular** to the direction of the magnetic field lines.

front_blocks.md: How can the direction of the **force** on a current-carrying conductor be reversed? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: The direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor can be reversed by:

- reversing the direction of the **magnetic field**

front_blocks.md: What is **Fleming's left-hand rule** used for? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: Fleming's left-hand rule is used to determine the direction of the **force** (thrust) on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, given the directions of the **current** and the **magnetic field**.

cards.front_md: What is **Fleming's left-hand rule** used for? **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md: Fleming's left-hand rule is used to determine the direction of the **force** (thrust) on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, given the directions of the **current** and the **magnetic field**.

front_blocks.md: State the quantity represented by each finger in Fleming's left-hand rule. **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: In Fleming's left-hand rule:

- the **thumb** points in the direction of the **force** (thrust) on the conductor
- the **first finger** points in the direction of the **magnetic field**
- the **second finger** points in the direction of the **current** (from positive to negative)

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The direction of the force on a current-carrying wire depends on the direction of the current and the magnetic field. **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: **True.**
The direction of the force on a current-carrying wire depends on the direction of the **current** and the direction of the **magnetic field**.
In Fleming's left-hand rule, the force, field and current are all **perpendicular** to each other.

front_blocks.md: What can the **motor effect** be used to create? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: The motor effect can be used to create a simple **d.c. electric motor**.
The force on a current-carrying coil causes it to **rotate** in a single direction.

cards.front_md: What can the **motor effect** be used to create? **(Extended Tier Only)**

front_blocks.md: Describe the structure of a simple **d.c. motor**. **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: A simple d.c. motor consists of:

- a **coil of wire** (which is free to rotate) between the poles of a **permanent magnet**
- a **split-ring commutator** and **brushes** connected to a source of d.c.

cards.front_md: Describe the structure of a simple **d.c. motor**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md:
A simple d.c. motor consists of:

- a **coil of wire** (which is free to rotate) between the poles of a **permanent magnet**
- a **split-ring commutator** and **brushes** connected to a source of d.c.

front_blocks.md: What causes the **coil** in a d.c. motor to **rotate**? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: As current flows through the coil, it produces a magnetic field which interacts with the external magnetic field.
Forces act in **opposite directions** on each side of the coil, causing a **turning effect**.

cards.front_md: What causes the **coil** in a d.c. motor to **rotate**? **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md:
As current flows through the coil, it produces a magnetic field which interacts with the external magnetic field.

Forces act in **opposite directions** on each side of the coil, causing a **turning effect**.

front_blocks.md: What does the **split-ring commutator** do to the current in a d.c. motor? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: The split-ring commutator **reverses** the direction of the current in the coil every **half turn**, so the forces on the coil continue to cause rotation in the **same direction**.

cards.front_md: What does the **split-ring commutator** do to the current in a d.c. motor? **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md: The split-ring commutator **reverses** the direction of the current in the coil every **half turn**, so the forces on the coil continue to cause rotation in the **same direction**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
When the coil of a d.c. motor is in the vertical position, no force acts on it. **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: **True.**
When the coil is vertical, the split ring is **no longer in contact** with the brushes, so no current flows and no forces act.
The **momentum** of the coil causes it to continue rotating until the split ring reconnects with the brushes.

cards.front_md:

The **momentum** of the coil causes it to continue rotating until the split ring reconnects with the brushes.

back_blocks.md: A **transformer** is a device used to **change** the size of an **alternating voltage** or current.
This is achieved using the generator effect.

front_blocks.md: Why is the core of a transformer made from **soft iron**? **(Extended Tier Only)**

front_blocks.md: What is a **step-up** transformer? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: A **step-up** transformer:

- **increases** the voltage of a power source `\left(V_{s} > V_{p}\right)`
- has **more turns** on the secondary coil than on the primary coil `\left(N_{s} > N_{p}\right)`

cards.front_md: What is a **step-up** transformer? **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md:

- **increases** the voltage of a power source `\left(V_{s} > V_{p}\right)`
- has **more turns** on the secondary coil than on the primary coil `\left(N_{s} > N_{p}\right)`

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A step-down transformer has fewer turns on the primary coil than the secondary coil. **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: **False.**
A **step-down** transformer has **fewer turns** on the **secondary** coil than on the primary coil `\left(N_{s} < N_{p}\right)`.
This **decreases** the voltage of the power source `\left(V_{s} < V_{p}\right)`.

cards.front_md:

cards.back_md:
**False.**

A **step-down** transformer has **fewer turns** on the **secondary** coil than on the primary coil `\left(N_{s} < N_{p}\right)`.

This **decreases** the voltage of the power source `\left(V_{s} < V_{p}\right)`.

cards.front_md: State the **transformer equation**. **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md:
The ratio of the voltages across the primary and secondary coils of a transformer is equal to the ratio of the number of turns on each coil:

$\frac{V_{p}}{V_{s}} = \frac{N_{p}}{N_{s}}$

Where:

- $V_{p}$ = voltage across the primary coil, in volts (V)
- $V_{s}$ = voltage across the secondary coil, in volts (V)
- $N_{p}$ = number of turns on the primary coil
- $N_{s}$ = number of turns on the secondary coil

front_blocks.md: How is the **output (secondary) voltage** of a transformer calculated? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: The output (secondary) voltage of a transformer is calculated using:
$V_{s} = V_{p} \times \frac{N_{s}}{N_{p}}$
This shows that the output voltage depends on:

- the **number of turns** on the primary and secondary coils
- the input (**primary**) voltage

- the input (**primary**) voltage

front_blocks.md: Define **ideal transformer**. **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: An **ideal transformer** is a transformer which is **100% efficient**, so the input power in the primary coil is equal to the output power of the secondary coil.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A transformer can increase both the voltage and the power output of a power source. **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Although transformers can increase the **voltage** of a power source, due to the law of **conservation of energy**, they cannot increase the **power** output.

front_blocks.md: Why is electricity transmitted at **high voltage**? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: Since $P = V I$, a high voltage means electricity can be transmitted at a **low current**.
A smaller current flowing through the power lines results in **less heat** being produced due to resistance in the wire.
This **reduces** the **energy loss** in the power lines, making the energy transfer more efficient.

cards.front_md: State the equation for the **power dissipated** in a wire due to resistance. **(Extended Tier Only)**
cards.back_md:
The power dissipated in a wire due to resistance is given by:

$P = I^{2} R$

Where:

- *P* = power, in watts (W)
- *I* = current, in amps (A)
- *R* = resistance, in ohms (Ω)

front_blocks.md: Where are **step-up** and **step-down** transformers used in high-voltage transmission? **(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: A **step-up** transformer is used to increase the voltage and decrease the current of electricity **before** transmission.
This ensures the same power transfer with a smaller current, so less thermal energy is lost due to resistance in the wire.
A **step-down** transformer is used to decrease the voltage and increase the current of electricity **after** transmission, because high-voltage electricity is dangerous for use in homes.
